list.listitem: Suspect smoke inhalation in patients with respiratory symptoms and in any patient found unconscious, found in a closed environment, or found with soot or burns in or near pharynx. C
Give high-flow oxygen at the scene and postexposure. C
Hydroxocobalamin should be given at the scene or in the emergency department if patient is found in a closed room or found unconscious. C
Intubation is needed for patients who show distress in the first 24 to 36 hours after a fire. C

background.definition: Smoke inhalation causes injury to pulmonary tissue associated with inhalation of smoke, toxic combustion products, heat damage, and asphyxiation.

list.listitem: Fire is the third leading cause of accidental death in all age groups in the United States. The incidence of fire-related deaths is annually 2.3 per 100,000 people.
The likelihood of smoke inhalation injury increases with the amount of body surface area burned.
A systematic review of 54 studies with over 400,000 burn patients found that 15% had inhalation injury, and that it increased mortality significantly (OR 3.2, 95% CI 2.5 to 4.3).
Household fires are the number one cause of smoke inhalation injury.

Wildfires caused by controlled burn and through wind-carried gas and particulate matter can be a significant cause of injury. Acute inhalation damage can occur, and this can result in long-term damage to respiratory tissue.
Exposure to cleanup sites where particulate matter is inhaled can cause acute and chronic damage to lung tissue.
Lung tissue can be damaged by zinc chloride (smoke bomb) inhalation during military training and on the battlefield.

Specific toxins are associated with different types of fires: wood smoke (carbon monoxide, hydrochloric acid, and phosgene); burning cotton or wool (carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide); and burning wood (acetic acid, alcohols, aldehydes, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, ketones, methane, and tars).

Gas injury can be divided into irritants and asphyxiants. Irritants include acrolein, aldehydes, ammonia, chlorine, hydrogen chloride, isocyanides, nitrogen oxide, phosgene, and sulfur dioxide. Carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrogen are classified as asphyxiants.
Steam from rapid cooling of the hot gas can damage the lower respiratory tract, causing thermal burns as the tissue rapidly cools.
Particulate matter of size less than one micron and irritating gas can lead to bronchospasm.
Gas can displace oxygen from the environment and produce hypoxia. Inhaled gases displace oxygen from red blood cells and create carboxyhemoglobin poisoning.
Carbon dioxide, hydrogen cyanide, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulfide can cause asphyxiation by displacing oxygen.

Hydrogen cyanide binds to the ferric ion and causes chemical asphyxiation by interfering with cellular metabolism. Hydrogen cyanide is found in polyurethane, wool, silk, nylon, nitrites, rubber, and paper products.
Smoke alarms are an inexpensive method of prevention. B
Respirators in cleanup sites can reduce long-term pulmonary damage. B
Clinical findings such as soot in the pharynx, singed nose hairs, respiratory compromise, or burns indicate a lower respiratory problem that may progress to respiratory distress. C
Check CXR and ABG in all patients who were found unconscious at the scene of a fire or exposed to smoke in a closed environment. B
Late impaired pulmonary function with smoke inhalation can occur. B
Have a high index of suspicion in patients with exposure to fires, smoke, and dust from cleanup sites who develop chronic lung symptoms. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Cough productive without soot or evidence of inhalation
Seizure, COPD, hyperglycemic coma, drugs, stroke
Other injuries, especially to head and neck

list.listitem: Patients may present with soot in nose or mouth, red sclera, thermal burns, or respiratory difficulty (wheezing, cough, dyspnea, tachypnea). Symptoms may take 72 hours to develop following inhalation.
Altered neurological signs like confusion, loss of consciousness, agitation, or confusion could signal toxicity from fumes, or poisoning from chemical inhalation.

Take history of how patient was found from first responders (i.e., conscious or not, in closed space or not). Patients with altered levels of consciousness and patients found in closed spaces are at higher risk for inhalation injury and cyanide toxicity.

Order CXR and ABG initially; monitor oxygen saturation. CXR may be misleading initially, so physical signs should be relied on for the primary assessment. Repeat CXR should be done in 4 to 6 hours. ABG can initially show higher oxygen due to treatment on the scene and should be rechecked if clinical signs change.
Pulmonary function test is used to access the chronic damage to the lung tissue, but use is limited since pre-exposure lung function is rarely known.

CT of the chest is valuable in assessing atelectasis and early adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). CT should be done in the emergency room if any wheezing or tachypnea is present. See chapter on ARDS for a more detailed discussion.

Fiberoptic laryngoscopy can be used if there is a question about whether intubation is required. Signs of soot, edema, and facial burns can be a reliable guide and coupled with the laryngoscopy evidence of edema of the larynx can validate the need for intubation.

Elevated cyanide levels are not necessary for pretreatment. Treatment should begin at the scene and be continued in the hospital, guided by cyanide levels following acute inhalation injuries. Cyanide level by automated gas chromatography can be used in the ED and later if needed to confirm toxicity.

Reduced erythrocyte cholinesterase activity is associated with inhalation exposure; however, it is not correlated with blood cyanide and carbon monoxide concentrations. The precise value of this test is uncertain.
Rarely, blood lead levels can be significantly elevated. Levels greater than 40 mcg/dL in adults should be treated. Routine testing for lead is not recommended.

Technetium-99m DTPA radioaerosol inhalation lung scintigraphy shows inhomogeneous distribution pattern and can identify severe small airway obstruction. Clearance rates are not reliable since the airflow is decreased and a relatively large amount of radiotracer could deposit in the airway instead of the alveoli. The interpretation should focus on the distribution pattern of radioactivity to evaluate small airways and the clearance to evaluate the alveoli.

Suspect inhalation injury in patients presenting with recent burn, smoke exposure, soot in the nose or mouth; patients found unconscious; and patients found in a closed space. Thermal burns on the face alert the need for intubation.
Respiratory difficulty, wheezing, cough, dyspnea, or tachypnea indicates lower respiratory tract involvement.
Altered neurological signs like confusion, loss of consciousness or agitation can signal hypoxia, cyanide poisoning, or toxicity from inhalation.
Provide high-flow oxygen at the scene and in the hospital when smoke inhalation is suspected. C
Continuous nebulized albuterol can improve lung function up to 48 hours after an acute smoke inhalation event in cases of stridor or respiratory distress. B
Hydroxocobalamin given at the scene or in the emergency room can reverse acute cyanide poisoning and should be used if there is soot in the face, mouth, or nose. B
Extensive burns or facial injury requires intubation or laryngoscopy to stabilize the airway. C

If cyanide exposure is suspected, give hydroxocobalamin (250 mg vials diluted with 100 mL of NaCl IV) over 15 minutes. Dose is 5 g for adults and 70 mg/kg for children, with the option to administer a second identical dose in the event of a transient or incomplete response. Dose is best given at the scene and can be repeated in the emergency department. Hydroxocobalamin was used in comatose and full arrest situations with good results.
Sodium nitrite or amyl nitrite is of less value than hydroxocobalamin in the cyanide exposure due to the decrease in oxygen caring capacity.
Lead exposure, if acute superimposed on inhalation, should be treated with removal from the lead exposed environment. Lead intoxication should be treated.

Inhaled anticoagulants in both pre-clinical and clinical studies were associated with a favorable effect on survival with severe smoke inhalation lung injury based on case reports, but well-designed studies are needed before routine use can be recommended.
See chapters on ARDS and Burns for specific guidance regarding treatment of comorbid conditions.

Provide high-flow oxygen at the scene and in the ED, and titrate oxygen saturation to at least 93% unless contraindicated in hypercapnic states such as preexisting Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Prognosis is poor in patients with extensive thermal burns, in patients who develop ARDS, and in the elderly and very young children. B
Significant inhalation adds 30% to 40% to the mortality of extensive burns due to late onset pneumonia. B
Patients with severe inhalation injury may have a higher risk of hospital-acquired pneumonia compared to those with mild inhalation injury. B
Comorbid conditions like COPD, asthma, or general poor health increase morbidity. B
